resolution: COLUMBUS QUEST. The Quest won the 1997-98 ABL championship 3 games to 2 over the Long Beach StingRays in a best-of-five, losing the first two on the road and then winning three straight at home in Columbus, clinching 86-81 on Sunday 15 March 1998. Valerie Still repeated as playoffs MVP with 25 points in the clincher.
reasoning: CONFIRMED AND CLOSED, not re-litigated. The contemporaneous AP game story (Spokesman-Review archive, 16 Mar 1998) reads: 'Columbus won its second straight American Basketball League title Sunday night, defeating the Long Beach StingRays 86-81. The Quest opened the best-of-5 series by losing twice...' APBR's own series table gives the same five games (LB 65-62, LB 71-61, COL 70-61, COL 68-53, COL 86-81), i.e. Long Beach won games 1-2 and Columbus games 3-4-5. The recorded 'APBR says Long Beach' was a misreading of that table, not a real disagreement between sources. Columbus therefore won both titles the ABL ever awarded (the 1998-99 season ended in the 22 Dec 1998 bankruptcy).

resolution: FOURTEEN franchises played in the WBL in 1979-80; only ELEVEN were still operating when the playoffs began. It depends on the date. (a) 14 clubs appear in the season's standings across three divisions: California Dreams, Chicago Hustle, Dallas Diamonds, Houston Angels, Iowa Cornets, Milwaukee Does, Minnesota Fillies, New Jersey Gems, New Orleans Pride, New York Stars, Philadelphia Fox, St. Louis Streak, San Francisco Pioneers, Washington Metros. (b) Two folded before Christmas 1979 - the Washington Metros after only 10 games (they suspended operations c. 21 Dec 1979) and the Philadelphia Fox at 2-8 (players waived c. 22 Dec 1979) - which leaves the 12 that played essentially full schedules, and that is the '12 clubs in three divisions' figure. (c) The league then revoked the California Dreams' franchise on 2 March 1980 after 28 games, so 11 clubs remained when the quarterfinals opened 17 March 1980. Also confirmed: the Washington Metros were NOT an expansion team - they were the relocated Dayton Rockettes (Dayton to Washington DC, playing also in Baltimore).
reasoning: APBR's franchise chronology lists 'Washington Metros 1979-80 [formerly Dayton Rockettes]' under In- and 'Dayton Rockettes [to Washington Metros]' under Out-, and marks Philadelphia and Washington with # ('disbanded or relocated during season'); its 1979-80 standings carry all 14 clubs, with Washington 3-7 and Philadelphia 2-8 and the footnote 'Philadelphia and Washington disbanded during the season'. Karra Porter's Mad Seasons supplies the dates from contemporaneous papers it cites in its notes ('Metros Suspend Operations', Washington Post, 21 Dec 1979; 'Metros Fold after Only 10 Games', Washington Star, 22 Dec 1979; 'Fox Folds; Players Put on Waivers', Philadelphia Inquirer, 22 Dec 1979) and states outright that 'on March 2, 1980, the league revoked the Dreams franchise after 28 games' - corroborated by its own aside that when California folded, Minnesota needed a fill-in opponent for its last home game. Fun While It Lasted independently says three 1979-80 clubs - California, Philadelphia and Washington DC - 'folded without completing their schedules'. So neither 12 nor 14 is wrong; a question must date-anchor. Basketball-Reference has no WBL data at all, so there is no rival Tier-1 table to check.

resolution: BEST-OF-FIVE, and the Houston Angels beat the Iowa Cornets 3 games to 2 - not 4-1. The five games: 17 Apr 1979 Houston 89-85, 20 Apr Houston 112-98, 23 Apr Iowa 110-101, 26 Apr Iowa 89-79, 1 May Houston 111-104. So the 111-104 score is the clincher of game five, played at the University of Houston before nearly 6,000 fans. Best-of-five was the WBL's finals format in all three seasons.
reasoning: The conflict was a misreading of APBR, which prints the WBL finals as a game log, not a series line: five dated game results with Houston winning three. Mad Seasons independently describes 'the 1979 championship game between the Houston Angels and the Iowa Cornets' at the University of Houston, with Iowa rallying late and blowing a designed last-second lob play - a decider, consistent with game five, not a 4-1 rout. Mad Seasons also settles the format directly for the last season: when Bryant Gumbel called the 1981 Nebraska-Dallas final 'a best of seven set' on the Today show, Porter interjects '(Actually, it was best of ﬁve.)' - and APBR's 1980-81 log likewise shows five games. Two independent statements of a 4-1 result could not be found anywhere; treat 4-1 as a table-reading error and retire it.

resolution: 1972, 1973 and 1974 - three consecutive national titles, then runner-up in 1975 and 1976. Finals: 1972 Immaculata 52-48 over West Chester at Normal, IL; 1973 Immaculata 59-52 over Queens (NY) at Flushing, NY; 1974 Immaculata 68-53 over Mississippi College at Manhattan, KS. The '1972-1976 window' is the two runner-up finishes to Delta State (90-81 in 1975, 69-64 in 1976) folded in with the titles.
reasoning: CONFIRMED AND CLOSED, not re-litigated. Two Tier-1 records agree: the NCAA's official AIAW results table (championship results with coaches, scores and sites, plus the full bracket lines - Immaculata 4-0 in each of 1972, 1973 and 1974) and the Naismith Hall of Fame's team page, enshrined as '1972-73-74 Immaculata College' (Class of 2014), which states Immaculata 'won the first of three consecutive Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women national championships' in spring 1972. Useful nuance from the NCAA table's own footnotes: 1969-71 were CIAW-sponsored and the 1972 event is marked DGWS-sponsored, so 1972 is the first title in the AIAW line - which is why some summaries garble the start of the run.

issue: When AAU women's national basketball actually ended
resolution: All three dates are true of different things, and the hypothesis in the corpus is correct. (1) 1969 - the last year the AAU champion was the de facto national champion of women's basketball: the CIAW held the first collegiate national championship in 1969 (West Chester over Western Carolina 65-39) and the NWIT also launched that year, so from 1969 the recognised national title moved to the college bodies (CIAW 1969-71, then AIAW/DGWS from 1972). (2) 1970 - not a real end date for the tournament. It is Wikipedia's sentence 'The AAU held women's basketball tournaments from 1926 through 1970', footnoted to Ikard 2005 p. 13, and it is refuted by the tournaments actually played afterwards. (3) The tournament itself kept going through the 1970s: Wayland Baptist won AAU national titles in 1970, 1971, 1974 and 1975 (its 10 AAU crowns, per the Naismith Hall, are impossible without them) and Wayland's own institutional history says it competed in AAU women's basketball 'between the 1948-49 season through the 1976-77 season'; the last three champions were a California club, Anna's Bananas (1977, 1978, 1979), with Ann Meyers an AAU All-American 1977-79 and AAU MVP for 1977-78. 1979 (Anna's Bananas over the Allentown Crestettes at Allentown, PA) is the last national tournament on the champions roll - held at MEDIUM confidence, see reasoning. Meanwhile the AAU itself had pivoted: its 1972 national convention voted to start girls 15-and-under and 18-and-under national tournaments, which is the AAU girls' basketball that still exists.
reasoning: The 1969 hinge is Tier-1: the NCAA's official AIAW results table lists CIAW-sponsored national champions for 1969, 1970 and 1971 before the AIAW line begins in 1972 - a collegiate national championship existed from 1969, which is exactly what If Not For Them means by 'the AAU Champion was the official national champion... from 1926 to 1969, when the CIAW and NWIT began hosting national championship events'. The post-1970 continuation is Tier-1 too and does not depend on If Not For Them: the Naismith Hall's Flying Queens page credits the team with 'ten national titles' in the AAU and enshrines it as the Flying Queens 'of 1948-1982', and the Hutcherson Flying Queens Foundation states Wayland competed in AAU basketball through the 1976-77 season while entering AIAW play from 1974 - both flatly incompatible with the tournament ending in 1970. Gale's Notable Sports Figures independently has Ann Meyers as an AAU All-American 1977-79 and AAU MVP 1977-78, i.e. senior AAU competition was still selecting All-Americans in 1979, and Carol Blazejowski played two post-college AAU seasons with the Allentown Crestettes (If Not For Them lists the Crestettes as the 1979 runner-up). Wikipedia's 1970 is a mis-summary of the very book that is the authority on this tournament: its footnote is Ikard, 'Just for Fun: The Story of AAU Women's Basketball' (Univ. of Arkansas Press, 2005), p. 13 - a page I could not open. WHY 1979 IS ONLY MEDIUM: the only sources putting the final tournament in 1979 are If Not For Them's champions roll (Tier 3) and bookseller blurbs for Ikard's book describing it as covering the tournament 'from its beginnings in 1926 to its 1979 demise', wording that appeared in search-result summaries but that I could NOT confirm on any page I actually opened - the publisher description at BiblioVault, Google Books and the University of Arkansas news release all omit any end year. I did not read the NYT archive, web.archive.org or newspapers.com. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: Ikard's book itself (p. 13 and its year-by-year AAU champions appendix), or the AAU's own national-championship records/convention minutes for 1979-1981, or a contemporaneous AP report of the 1979 tournament at Allentown identifying it as the last (or of an AAU senior women's national tournament in 1980, which would refute 1979).

issue: WBL team count for the final 1980-81 season
resolution: NINE teams began the 1980-81 season and EIGHT finished it - both numbers are right, at different dates, so the 'self-contradictory' source is not actually wrong. The nine: Chicago Hustle, Dallas Diamonds, Minnesota Fillies, Nebraska Wranglers (the relocated California Dreams), New England Gulls, New Jersey Gems, New Orleans Pride, St. Louis Streak, San Francisco Pioneers. The New England Gulls died mid-season: unpaid for months, the players walked off after a 15 January 1981 game in Portland, Maine, and on 20 JANUARY 1981 commissioner Sherwin Fischer revoked the franchise (unanimously ratified by the Board of Governors) with the Gulls 2-10. From 20 Jan 1981 onward the league had eight clubs. A further wrinkle if a question needs the very end: after their own walkout (20-21 March 1981) the Minnesota Fillies were suspended in the closing weeks, so fewer than eight were operating in April, and the Nebraska Wranglers beat Dallas 3-2 in the final best-of-five, ending 20 April 1981.
reasoning: APBR's 1980-81 line lists exactly nine clubs (CHH DLD MNF NBW NEG* NJG NOP SLS SFP) with the New England Gulls marked as disbanded during the season and standing at 2-10 in a league where everyone else played 35-37 games; its chronology also shows Nebraska as 'formerly California Dreams' and New England as the only 1980-81 expansion entry. Mad Seasons gives the mechanism and the exact date: the Tampa Bay franchise granted to founder Bill Byrne was transferred to New England investor Joseph Reither ('eight of the nine had approved Reither's application'), the Gulls never paid their players, and 'On January 20, 1981, Fischer revoked the New England Gulls franchise. Reither's conduct, he wrote, had 'resulted in substantial loss of credibility on the part of the league on a national level.' The wbl Board of Governors unanimously ratified Fischer's decision.' Same book dates the players' abandonment to the 15 Jan 1981 Portland game and the Fillies' walkout to Friday 20 March 1981 (citing 'No Bed of Roses for Suspended Fillies', Minneapolis Star, 24 Mar 1981); Fun While It Lasted independently says 'the league lost another team in mid-season when the New England Gulls went belly up.' Prose-vs-list is a snapshot-date artefact, not a source error - a question can safely ask which nine clubs began the WBL's final season, or state that it finished with eight.

resolution: Same finding as the other Immaculata entry: titles 1972, 1973, 1974; runner-up 1975 and 1976. This duplicate conflict entry can be closed with it.
reasoning: CONFIRMED AND CLOSED. The corpus records this issue twice ('Immaculata's AIAW title years' and 'Immaculata's AIAW years (previously open)'); both are settled by the same two Tier-1 records - the NCAA's official AIAW championship results table (three titles with scores and sites, plus 1975 and 1976 runner-up lines) and the Naismith Hall of Fame team page for '1972-73-74 Immaculata College' (Class of 2014, '3x AIAW National Champion', 35-game win streak, 60 wins in three seasons). No source I opened supports titles in 1975 or 1976. Recommend de-duplicating the conflicts array.

issue: The Edmonton Grads' actual won-lost record
resolution: The three figures count different things, and the discrepancy is documented rather than mysterious. (1) 502-20 in 522 games (96.2%) is the traditional/'official' figure. Per M. Ann Hall, as summarised by The Canadian Encyclopedia, that 522 total INCLUDES the games played by the McDougall (MacDougall) Commercial junior and senior HIGH SCHOOL teams in 1915-1922 - the feeder teams, before the Grads proper - as well as the Grads' own games, plus there are further discrepancies in the surviving records for 1922-1940. (2) 392-20 in 412 games (95.1%) is historian M. Ann Hall's recount in 'The Grads Are Playing Tonight!' (2011): the Grads' own games only, with the undocumentable/double-counted games stripped out. Her publisher, the University of Alberta Press, states it as 'they played over 400 official games, losing only 20'. (3) 412-20 in 432 games is the City of Edmonton Archives' online exhibit ('They won 412 out of 432 games played, with only 20 losses', team dated 1915-1940). The Archives publish no methodology; note that 412 is exactly Hall's TOTAL GAMES figure and 432 = 412 + 20, so this reads as Hall's game total re-used as a win total with the losses added on - a likely transcription chain, but that is my inference, not a sourced finding. A fourth figure exists: Canada's History magazine says 'According to team records (which are supported by newspaper accounts), the Grads played 428 official games between 1915 and 1940... 20 is often cited' as losses. IMPORTANT: the split is NOT league-vs-exhibition. The Grads had no league - virtually every game was a challenge or exhibition (Alberta and Western Canadian titles, Canadian championships, the Underwood International Trophy series against the US AAU champion, and four European tours). The real axes are (a) do the 1915-22 school-team games count, and (b) how many 1922-40 games can be documented. Safe phrasing for a question: the traditional record is 502-20 (about 96%) and the win percentage - roughly 95-96% either way - is what is not in dispute.
reasoning: The Canadian Encyclopedia states the reconciliation explicitly: 'Traditionally, the Grads are considered to have played 522 games in total, winning 502 and losing only 20. However, these numbers have been challenged by M. Ann Hall... According to Hall, the Grads played over 400 games during their 25 years as a team, losing 20. She explains that the higher total (522) includes games played by the MacDougall Commercial junior and senior high school teams in the period from 1915 to 1922, as well as those played by the Grads themselves. Moreover, there are some discrepancies in the records pertaining to games played between 1922 and 1940. While a definite number may never be achieved...' Hall's own publisher independently states 'over 400 official games, losing only 20', which corroborates the ~412 magnitude and refutes 522 as her count. The precise 392-20-in-412 breakdown is Wikipedia reporting Hall ('proposes that the Grads played a total of 412 games, with 392 wins and 20 losses... 95.1%') - an index citation to a book page I could not open, so the exact split stays medium confidence while the direction of Hall's correction is solid. The City of Edmonton Archives figure was read directly off the Archives' own exhibit page. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: Hall's game-by-game accounting in 'The Grads Are Playing Tonight!' (Univ. of Alberta Press, 2011) and the underlying Grads / J. Percy Page scrapbooks and game records held at the City of Edmonton Archives - the same holdings the Archives' exhibit is drawn from. Absent those, The Canadian Encyclopedia's own verdict stands: a definite number may never be achieved, so do not write a question that turns on the raw count without attributing it ('the team's official record').

resolution: There is no single founding year - the honest answer names the milestone. 1914: J. Percy Page introduced girls' basketball at Edmonton's McDougall Commercial High School and its team won the city high school league and the Alberta title. 1915: the graduating students asked Page to keep coaching them and the Commercial Graduates club was formed - which is why the traditional span, used by the City of Edmonton Archives, The Canadian Encyclopedia and the team's own record-keeping, is 1915-1940. 1917: the year The Canadian Encyclopedia says the Edmonton Grads 'officially began competing'. 1922: first Canadian national championship, and the cutoff for the 'official' 38 Grads - the club's recognised member list only counts players from 1922 to 1940. 1940: disbanded, not in dispute. The 1912 in the Wikipedia infobox is NOT a team date: 1912 is when Page took a post in Edmonton to introduce commercial training into the city's high schools. Do not print a bare founding year; say '1915-1940' for the club, 1914 for the school team, 1922 for the first national title.
reasoning: Four independent sources agree the team span is 1915-1940 and none supports 1912: the City of Edmonton Archives exhibit ('an amateur women's basketball team that played from 1915 to 1940'), Canada's History ('the Grads played 428 official games between 1915 and 1940, when they disbanded'; Page introduced girls' basketball at McDougall Commercial in 1914 'through his physical education classes'), and The Canadian Encyclopedia, which supplies the finer grain - first McDougall Commercial High School team 1914, Grads 'officially began competing' 1917, and 'the (official) 38 members... only includes players from 1922 to 1940'. Wikipedia's own body text says competitive play began 1914 at the school and the club was established on the players' graduation in mid-1915, so the article's 1912 infobox value contradicts its own prose - the classic infobox-vs-text artefact rather than a genuine source conflict. The 1912 date matches Page's arrival in Edmonton to set up commercial training (he was McDougall Commercial's principal from 1920), which is a lead from a Tier-3 index and would want his own biography or Edmonton Public Schools records to nail down; either way it is a fact about the coach, not the team. Remaining soft spot: 1915 vs 1917 for 'began competing' is a live distinction between reputable sources - phrase around it.
